Bring to a boil over medium-high heat, then reduce to a brisk simmer. Cook uncovered for 15–20 minutes, stirring occasionally, until lentils have completely dissolved into the tomatoes and the mixture is thick and smooth. The lentils will turn from orange-red to golden yellow as they cook.

In a small pan or ladle, heat mustard oil over high heat until it begins to smoke lightly (smoking point neutralizes mustard oil's harsh raw flavour). Add mustard seeds and wait for them to pop and splutter. Add cumin seeds — they will darken within 10 seconds. Add dried red chili and fry for 5 seconds. The entire tarka happens in under 30 seconds — have all spices measured and ready before heating the oil.

In the same dal pot, if including raw onion sauté it until golden in 1 tbsp oil, then combine with the dal. Pour the sizzling tarka directly over the surface of the dal in one decisive move. The oil will hit the dal with a dramatic hiss. Stir to incorporate. Add lemon juice, taste and adjust salt. The acidity brightens and lifts the entire dish — add it at the end, never during cooking.
fr-matcha-castella: Warm the whole eggs (in their shells) in hot tap water for 5 minutes. Combine the warmed eggs, sugar, and honey in the bowl of a stand mixer (or use a hand mixer). Beat at high speed for 8-10 minutes until the mixture is very pale, tripled in volume, and holds a thick ribbon that dissolves back in about 10 seconds when the whisk is lifted. The warm eggs help dissolve the sugar and retain air. Do not rush this stage — the aerated egg foam is the only leavener in castella.

Sift the bread flour and matcha powder together twice to ensure even distribution. Sift one-third of the matcha-flour over the egg foam and fold with a large spatula in slow, sweeping movements from the bottom of the bowl — cut down the center, sweep along the bottom, fold up over the top. Rotate the bowl and repeat. Add the remaining flour in two more additions. Fold in the warm milk with the last addition. Stop as soon as no dry streaks remain — every additional fold deflates the foam.

Line a 21 x 10 cm loaf tin with baking paper (parchment), leaving overhang on all sides. Pour in the batter and gently tap the tin on the counter twice to release large air bubbles. Run a skewer through the batter in a figure-eight motion to break any visible bubble clusters. Bake at 160 C (320 F) for 50-60 minutes, rotating once at 30 minutes. The top should be a deep, dark brown — this is correct for castella, not a sign of overcooking. A skewer inserted in the center should come out clean.

Immediately upon removing from the oven, lift the castella out by the paper overhang and wrap the entire loaf tightly in plastic wrap while still hot. The steam trapped inside creates the characteristic moist, tight crumb of authentic castella. Place wrapped in the refrigerator for at least 1 hour (overnight is better). Slice into 2 cm rectangles with a wet knife, wiping the blade between cuts for clean edges.
fr-matcha-cheesecake: Crush the digestive biscuits in a food processor to a fine, even sand — no large chunks or sandy dust, a uniform medium crumb. Alternatively, seal them in a zip-lock bag and roll with a rolling pin. Stir in the melted butter until every crumb is evenly coated — the mixture should look like damp sand that just clumps when pressed. Tip into the base of a 20 cm (8 inch) springform tin lined with baking parchment. Use the flat base of a glass to press the crumbs into a compact, even, level layer. Refrigerate for 15 minutes to set the butter.

Submerge the gelatin sheets in cold water for 5–8 minutes until completely floppy and translucent. Lift them out and squeeze out the excess water — the gelatin should weigh almost nothing in your palm. Set aside. For powdered gelatin, sprinkle it over 2 tablespoons of cold water and leave it to absorb into a firm sponge before heating. Gelatin enables the no-bake filling to hold its shape while maintaining a creamy, barely-set texture rather than a rubbery one.

Sift the matcha powder into a small bowl — sifting is non-negotiable, as matcha clumps badly and will leave green specks in the filling if not dispersed. Add the hot water (about 70–80°C, just off the boil — not boiling, which degrades the vivid green and the delicate flavor). Using a small whisk or matcha chasen, whisk in tight 'M' or 'W' motions until the powder is fully dissolved into a smooth, vivid green paste with no lumps. Melt the squeezed gelatin in 2 tablespoons of warm cream in a small saucepan over very low heat, swirling until dissolved. Stir the gelatin into the matcha paste.

Beat the room-temperature cream cheese with the icing sugar and lemon juice until completely smooth and lump-free — 2 minutes with a hand mixer. Fold in the matcha-gelatin paste until evenly colored. In a cold bowl, whip the cold heavy cream to firm peaks. Fold the whipped cream into the matcha cream cheese mixture in three additions, from the bottom up, cutting and folding gently to retain the volume. The final filling should be airy, vivid green, and hold a soft peak.

Pour the filling over the chilled biscuit base and smooth the top with an offset spatula, spreading to the edges. Tap the tin gently on the counter twice to settle any air bubbles. Cover with cling film and refrigerate for a minimum of 4 hours, or overnight — the gelatin needs time to set fully and the flavors to develop. Before serving, dust the surface lightly with sifted matcha powder through a fine-mesh sieve. Release the springform and cut with a hot, wiped knife for clean slices.
fr-matcha-cheesecake-gf: Crush the gluten-free biscuits in a food processor to a fine, even sand — no large chunks or sandy dust, a uniform medium crumb. Alternatively, seal them in a zip-lock bag and roll with a rolling pin. Stir in the melted butter until every crumb is evenly coated — the mixture should look like damp sand that just clumps when pressed. Tip into the base of a 20 cm (8 inch) springform tin lined with baking parchment. Use the flat base of a glass to press the crumbs into a compact, even, level layer. Refrigerate for 15 minutes to set the butter.

Submerge the gelatin sheets in cold water for 5–8 minutes until completely floppy and translucent. Lift them out and squeeze out the excess water — the gelatin should weigh almost nothing in your palm. Set aside. For powdered gelatin, sprinkle it over 2 tablespoons of cold water and leave it to absorb into a firm sponge before heating. Gelatin enables the no-bake filling to hold its shape while maintaining a creamy, barely-set texture rather than a rubbery one.

Sift the matcha powder into a small bowl — sifting is non-negotiable, as matcha clumps badly and will leave green specks in the filling if not dispersed. Add the hot water (about 70–80°C, just off the boil — not boiling, which degrades the vivid green and the delicate flavor). Using a small whisk or matcha chasen, whisk in tight 'M' or 'W' motions until the powder is fully dissolved into a smooth, vivid green paste with no lumps. Melt the squeezed gelatin in 2 tablespoons of warm cream in a small saucepan over very low heat, swirling until dissolved. Stir the gelatin into the matcha paste.

Beat the room-temperature cream cheese with the icing sugar and lemon juice until completely smooth and lump-free — 2 minutes with a hand mixer. Fold in the matcha-gelatin paste until evenly colored. In a cold bowl, whip the cold heavy cream to firm peaks. Fold the whipped cream into the matcha cream cheese mixture in three additions, from the bottom up, cutting and folding gently to retain the volume. The final filling should be airy, vivid green, and hold a soft peak.

Pour the filling over the chilled gluten-free biscuits base and smooth the top with an offset spatula, spreading to the edges. Tap the tin gently on the counter twice to settle any air bubbles. Cover with cling film and refrigerate for a minimum of 4 hours, or overnight — the gelatin needs time to set fully and the flavors to develop. Before serving, dust the surface lightly with sifted matcha powder through a fine-mesh sieve. Release the springform and cut with a hot, wiped knife for clean slices.
fr-matcha-ice-cream: Sift the matcha powder into a wide, shallow bowl to break up any clumps — matcha is finely milled and prone to lumping. Add 3 tablespoons (about 45g) of the measured whole milk, warm but not hot (around 60 C). Using a bamboo chasen (matcha whisk) or a small balloon whisk, whisk the matcha and milk in rapid 'M'-and 'W'-shaped strokes until a smooth, lump-free paste forms. Add the remaining milk gradually, whisking to maintain smoothness. Matcha paste must be completely homogeneous before being added to the custard — a single undissolved lump will leave a bitter green streak in the finished ice cream.

In a medium heatproof bowl, whisk the egg yolks and caster sugar together vigorously for about 2 minutes until the mixture has turned pale, noticeably thickened, and falls from the whisk in a slow, wide ribbon. This is the ribbon stage — it indicates that enough air and emulsification have occurred to give the custard body. The yolks will be ready when they have doubled in volume, turned from deep orange to pale cream-yellow, and the ribbon holds on the surface for 3 seconds before sinking. This step also helps buffer the yolks against scrambling when the hot matcha milk is added.

Combine the matcha milk and remaining heavy cream in a medium saucepan. Heat over medium heat, stirring occasionally, until the mixture just begins to steam and small bubbles appear at the edge — about 75 C. Do not boil. Slowly pour about one-third of the hot matcha cream into the yolk mixture while whisking constantly — this is tempering: gradually raising the egg temperature to prevent scrambling. Pour the tempered yolk mixture back into the saucepan with the remaining hot cream. Cook over medium-low heat, stirring constantly with a silicone spatula in figure-eight patterns and scraping the bottom and corners, until the custard reaches 82 C and coats the back of a spoon cleanly. Add the pinch of salt. Immediately strain through a fine-mesh sieve into a clean bowl set over an ice bath.

Cool the custard base completely over the ice bath, stirring occasionally, then refrigerate for at least 2 hours or overnight until it is thoroughly chilled — around 4 C. Churn in an ice cream machine according to the manufacturer's instructions until the ice cream is the consistency of thick, scoopable soft-serve (about 20 to 25 minutes). Transfer to a chilled container, press parchment paper directly onto the surface to prevent ice crystal formation, and freeze for at least 3 hours before scooping. For a no-churn version: whip 200g of the heavy cream to medium peaks separately, fold into the chilled custard, and freeze in a loaf pan for 5 hours.
fr-mexican-esquites: Heat a wide, dry cast-iron skillet or heavy pan over the highest possible heat until you can hold your palm 5cm above the surface for only 1–2 seconds. Add the butter, let it foam and begin to brown, then add the corn kernels in a single, uncrowded layer — you may need to do this in two batches. Do not stir for 2 full minutes. Let the bottom layer of corn make hard contact with the hot pan and char. Then toss once and let it sit for another 90 seconds. The goal is visible black charring on some kernels with others remaining golden — a variety of char is more interesting than uniform browning.

While the corn is still hot, transfer to a bowl. Add the crema, mayonnaise, lime juice, chile powder, and sliced scallions. Toss immediately — the heat from the corn will warm the dressing and help it coat every kernel. Taste and adjust: more lime for brightness, more chile for heat, a pinch of salt if needed. The dressing should be creamy, tangy, and spicy — each bite should have all four elements simultaneously.

Transfer to cups or a serving bowl. Scatter the crumbled cotija generously over the top — it should look like a snow of salty cheese. Add the chopped cilantro. Finish with an extra dusting of chile powder on top for visual contrast and an additional hit of heat. Serve immediately — this is a hot dish and the textural contrast of the charred kernels diminishes as they cool.
fr-middle-eastern-basbousa: Combine the semolina, sugar, and baking powder in a large bowl. Add the yoghurt, melted butter, and rose water. Mix well with a spatula until fully combined — the batter will be thick and grainy, not smooth. Unlike a standard cake batter, it should hold its shape when mounded. Grease a 23x23cm baking pan. Spread the batter evenly with a wet spatula, pressing it into an even layer about 2cm thick. Let rest 15 minutes to allow the semolina to hydrate.

Preheat oven to 180°C (350°F). Score the rested batter into diamond or square shapes with a wet knife, cutting almost all the way through. Press a whole blanched almond into the center of each piece. Bake for 25-30 minutes until the top is golden and the edges are beginning to pull away from the pan. The surface should look slightly firm and dry.

Combine sugar and water in a small saucepan. Bring to a boil over medium heat, stirring only until the sugar dissolves. Once boiling, stop stirring and cook for 5-7 minutes until slightly thickened. Add the lemon juice and cook for 1 more minute (the acid prevents crystallization). Remove from heat and stir in the orange blossom water. The syrup should be ready just before the cake comes out of the oven — it must go hot onto hot.

Pour the hot syrup slowly and evenly over the hot basbousa in a thin, steady stream. Pour in the scored lines first, then over the whole surface. The cake will sizzle and absorb the syrup immediately. You should use all the syrup. Allow to rest at room temperature for at least 30 minutes until fully absorbed and the cake has cooled slightly. Cut along the score lines to serve. Basbousa improves after several hours as the flavors meld.
fr-middle-eastern-mujaddara: Heat the olive oil in a wide, heavy-bottomed pan over medium-high heat. Add all the sliced onions — the pan will be very full. Cook, stirring every 3–4 minutes, for 35–45 minutes. The onions will shrink dramatically, releasing water first, then slowly browning as the water evaporates. In the last 10 minutes, increase heat to high and stir more frequently as the onions caramelize. The goal is deeply browned, almost crispy onions that are sweet and complex. Remove two-thirds of the onions and set aside as the topping. Leave one-third in the pan.

In the same pan with the remaining one-third of the caramelized onions, add the ground cumin, coriander, and allspice. Stir for 30 seconds. Add the rinsed lentils and the water. Bring to a boil, then reduce to a gentle simmer. Cook for 15 minutes until the lentils are partially tender but still have a slight bite — they are not done yet. Season generously with salt.

Add the rinsed basmati rice to the partially cooked lentils and stir to combine. Check the water level — there should be enough to just cover the mixture by 1cm. Add a splash more if needed. Bring to a boil, then cover tightly and reduce heat to the lowest setting. Cook for 15 minutes. Do not lift the lid. Remove from heat and let steam, covered, for 10 more minutes. Fluff with a fork. The lentils and rice should be cooked through and have absorbed all the liquid.

Plate the mujaddara in a wide, shallow bowl or deep plate. Pile the reserved caramelized onions on top — do not stir them in; the contrast of the soft, spiced rice-and-lentil base with the crispy, sweet onion crown is the dish. Serve with plain yogurt, a salad of chopped tomato and cucumber, and gluten-free flatbread.
fr-misir-wot: Place the finely minced onions in a heavy-bottomed pot with no oil over medium heat. Stir every 2–3 minutes for 20–25 minutes — the onions will first release water and steam in it, then dry out and begin to colour. The goal is a reduced, dark-tan, sweet-smelling onion base. This dry caramelization without fat is the traditional Ethiopian method (called 'dry frying' the onions) that gives misir wot its characteristic depth. The onions should shrink to about one-third of their starting volume and turn a warm golden-brown before any fat is added.

Add the niter kibbeh to the caramelized onions and stir until melted. Add the berbere, garlic, and ginger. Stir vigorously and cook over medium heat for 4–6 minutes, stirring constantly — the berbere will foam slightly as it hits the hot fat, then the fat will begin to separate at the edges as the spices cook. The mixture will become a very thick, dark, fragrant paste. The cooking of berbere in fat is non-negotiable: raw berbere tastes sharp and acrid; bloomed berbere tastes rounded, deep, and complex.

Add the rinsed red lentils to the spiced base and stir to coat them in the dark paste — they should turn a dark brick-red immediately. Add the water or stock and the salt. Stir to combine, scraping any stuck paste from the bottom. Bring to a boil over high heat, stirring occasionally. Reduce to a medium simmer, cover partially, and cook for 20–25 minutes, stirring every 5 minutes to prevent sticking. Red lentils cook quickly and dissolve completely — misir wot is not chunky; the lentils should entirely melt into the sauce to form a thick, uniform, porridge-like texture.

Add the lemon juice and stir through. Taste and adjust: more berbere for heat and depth, more salt for savory presence, more lemon for brightness. Let the stew rest for 5 minutes off the heat — it will thicken slightly as it sits. Serve on gluten-free flatbread: spoon the misir wot in a mound on top of a large round of gluten-free flatbread and allow it to spread and be absorbed. The gluten-free flatbread tears into pieces that scoop the stew. Traditionally served alongside other wots on a single large shared plate.
fr-miso-black-cod: Combine white miso, mirin, sake, and sugar in a small saucepan over medium-low heat. Stir until the sugar dissolves and the mixture is smooth and slightly warmed (do not boil). Remove from heat and cool completely to room temperature. The marinade should be thick and spreadable, slightly thicker than heavy cream.

Pat the cod fillets completely dry with paper towels. Coat the flesh side generously with marinade, pressing it into the fish surface. A thin layer on the skin side is fine. Place in a zip-lock bag or container, making sure each piece is well-coated. Refrigerate for 2–3 days (72 hours for the full effect). The longer the marination, the deeper the flavor penetration and the more dramatic the miso lacquer during cooking.

Remove fillets from the marinade and gently scrape off the excess with a spoon or your fingers — do not rinse. Excess miso will burn, not caramelize. Place skin-side down on a foil-lined baking sheet lightly oiled. Broil 15–18 cm from the element for 8–12 minutes, watching constantly. The miso should caramelize to a deep golden-mahogany — not burnt, not pale.

Transfer each fillet carefully — they are extremely delicate — to a warm plate using a wide spatula. Add a small pile of sliced pickled ginger beside the fish. Grate a tiny amount of yuzu or lemon zest over the top. Serve immediately with steamed rice and a simple cucumber vinegar salad to cut the richness.
fr-miso-butter-salmon-green-beans: Heat the oven to 425°F (220°C) with a rack in the upper-middle position. In a small bowl, mash the miso, softened butter, honey and grated garlic with a fork until completely smooth and uniform.
On a rimmed sheet pan, toss the green beans with the oil and 1/2 tsp kosher salt and spread them out. Roast for 8 minutes to give them a head start.

Pat the salmon dry. Push the beans to the edges of the pan and lay the fillets skin-side down in the center. Spread the miso butter thickly over the tops and sides of the fillets. Roast 9–12 minutes, depending on thickness, until the salmon flakes easily and is opaque at the center or reads 145°F (63°C) in the thickest part. If the tops are pale, switch to the broiler for the final 1–2 minutes, watching constantly — miso burns quickly.

Drizzle the rice vinegar over the green beans and toss them in the melted miso butter on the pan. Plate the salmon with the beans, spoon over any remaining pan juices, and scatter with scallions and sesame seeds. Serve with steamed rice if you like.
fr-miso-glazed-eggplant: Halve the eggplants lengthwise. Using a sharp paring knife, score the cut face in a deep crosshatch pattern — cut about two-thirds into the flesh at 1 cm intervals in both directions without piercing the skin. This scoring is critical: it allows heat to penetrate and sesame oil to seep into the flesh, preventing steam from splitting the skin and dramatically shortening the roasting time. Press the cut face lightly to open the grid slightly.

Brush the scored cut face generously with sesame oil, working the oil into the crosshatch cuts with the brush. Flip and brush a thin layer over the skin side as well. The sesame oil serves double duty: it prevents sticking and imparts a deep, nutty fragrance that suffuses the flesh during roasting. Line a baking tray with foil and place eggplant halves cut-side down.

Roast cut-side down in a 220°C (425°F) oven for 12–15 minutes, until the flesh is completely tender when pierced with a chopstick or skewer and the cut faces have taken on a light gold color from contact with the tray. This initial roasting collapses the air pockets in the spongy eggplant flesh and drives out moisture, which concentrates the flavor and creates the right base for the glaze to adhere to. Do not rush this step — underdone eggplant will have a bitter, spongy bite.

While the eggplant roasts, combine white miso, mirin, sake, and sugar in a small saucepan over very low heat. Whisk constantly as the mixture warms — the goal is just to dissolve the sugar and bring everything into a smooth, homogeneous paste, not to cook it. The glaze should be warm, fluid, and spreadable, the consistency of thick yogurt. Remove from heat as soon as it is smooth. Taste: it should be deeply savory, sweetly balanced, and intensely fragrant.

Flip the roasted eggplant halves so the cut face is now up. Spoon the dengaku glaze generously over each half, spreading it to the edges with the back of the spoon. The layer should be thick enough to be opaque — roughly 3–4mm — so it caramelizes and chars slightly rather than burning off thin. Do not be timid: a thick, generous glaze is what makes this dish.

Broil the glazed eggplant halves under a hot broiler (or salamander) for 3–5 minutes, watching constantly. The glaze should bubble, then caramelize to deep amber-brown with slightly charred edges and spots — this Maillard browning and mild caramelization is the defining character of dengaku. Remove from the broiler and let rest for 1 minute on the tray. Transfer to serving plates, scatter toasted sesame seeds generously, and finish with sliced scallion. Serve immediately while the eggplant is still trembling-soft and the glaze is warm.
fr-miso-glazed-salmon: Whisk together the white miso, mirin, sake, and sugar until fully smooth and the sugar has dissolved. The marinade should be a pale caramel paste that flows like thick honey. Taste it: it should be intensely savory and sweet, with the faint sting of alcohol — the sake and mirin will carry the volatile top notes away as the fish broils, leaving the miso caramelized and fragrant.

Season the salmon lightly with salt, then coat each fillet on all sides with the miso marinade. Place in a shallow dish or zip-lock bag, making sure the marinade contacts every surface. Refrigerate for at least 1 hour and up to 24 hours — the longer the rest, the deeper the savory penetration and the more intense the caramelized crust. Wipe off the excess marinade before broiling; any thick layer will burn before the fish cooks.

Position an oven rack about 15 cm from the broiler element and preheat the broiler to maximum. Line a baking sheet with foil and lightly oil it. Wipe the excess marinade from the salmon, place skin-side down, and broil 8–12 minutes depending on thickness — no flipping needed. Watch continuously: the miso sugars move from golden to burnt in under a minute at this heat. The skin should crisp and the glaze should bubble, bronze, and develop dark caramelized spots at the edges.

Slide the fillets onto warm plates using a thin spatula. The skin may stick to the foil — use the spatula to separate it cleanly. Scatter thinly sliced scallion greens over the top. Serve immediately with steamed short-grain rice and a small mound of pickled ginger or a wedge of sudachi if available.
fr-miso-roasted-sweet-potato: Preheat the oven to 180 C (355 F). Place the whole, unpeeled sweet potatoes directly on the oven rack with a foil-lined tray below to catch drips. Roast for 55–75 minutes depending on size (a chopstick pressed into the thickest part should meet no resistance). The skin will blister and deflate; a dark, caramelised syrup will drip from the ends.

While the potatoes roast, combine the softened butter, white miso, and mirin in a small bowl. Stir vigorously until completely smooth and homogenous. The mixture will be a pale amber paste. Set aside at room temperature.

Split each sweet potato lengthwise with a sharp knife — but not quite all the way through. Press the two ends toward each other to open up the split and create a cavity. Spoon or pipe a generous amount of the miso butter into the cavity. Finish under the grill (broiler) at high heat for 3–4 minutes until the glaze is bubbling and caramelised. Scatter flaky salt, sesame seeds, and spring onion.
fr-mochi-daifuku: Divide the anko (bean paste) into portions — approximately 25g per daifuku. Flatten each portion into a disc in your palm. Place a hulled strawberry point-down in the center and wrap the anko up around it, pinching to seal at the base of the strawberry. The strawberry tip should just be visible or barely covered. Refrigerate wrapped strawberries for 15 minutes to firm.

Whisk shiratamako, sugar, and water together in a microwave-safe bowl until smooth with no lumps. Cover loosely with plastic wrap and microwave on high for 2 minutes. Remove, stir thoroughly with a wet spatula, then microwave for a further 1 minute. Stir again — the mochi should be fully translucent with no white, opaque patches. If white patches remain, microwave in 30-second bursts, stirring each time. Alternatively, steam in a covered steamer for 20 minutes, stirring halfway through.

Dust a work surface generously with katakuriko. Turn the hot mochi out onto the dusted surface — it will be extremely sticky and very hot, so work quickly. Dust the top and your hands. Divide into equal portions (approximately 40g each) using a dusted dough cutter or scissors. Stretch each portion into a disc about 10 cm wide. Place an anko-wrapped strawberry in the center, point-down. Gather the mochi edges up and over, pinching firmly to seal at the base. Pinch point downward. Dust the finished daifuku with more katakuriko to prevent sticking.
fr-mochi: Combine the glutinous rice flour and sugar in a microwave-safe bowl. Add the water gradually while stirring with a spatula until completely smooth and lump-free. The batter will be thin — like very thick cream — and should pour off the spatula in a slow, even sheet. Pass it through a fine strainer if any lumps remain. Cover loosely with microwave-safe plastic wrap or a damp paper towel.

Microwave the covered batter on HIGH for 2 minutes. Remove, uncover, and stir vigorously — the outer edge will have cooked to a translucent, rubbery mass while the centre remains white and liquid. Stir to combine them, re-cover, and microwave again for 1 to 2 minutes until the entire mass is translucent, pulling away from the bowl sides, and glistening. Stir well between each burst. The dough should look uniformly glossy and slightly translucent, not chalky or opaque. Total microwave time: 4 to 6 minutes in 1-2 minute bursts.

Dust a clean work surface generously with cornstarch. Turn the hot mochi out onto the surface and dust the top as well. Let it cool for 5 to 10 minutes — it should be warm but comfortable to handle. Do not let it cool completely: cold mochi becomes stiff and tears when portioned. Divide into 8 equal pieces using a bench scraper or a knife dusted with cornstarch. Flatten each piece into a round disc about 8 cm in diameter, working quickly.

Roll a tablespoon-sized ball of anko between your palms to a smooth sphere and place it at the centre of each mochi disc. Gather the edges of the mochi up around the filling and pinch firmly together at the top, rotating and pleating as you go, until the seam is completely sealed with no filling visible. Pinch the seam tightly — a loose seam opens during handling. Turn seam-side down and roll gently between cupped palms to smooth the surface. Roll in kinako to coat. Arrange seam-side down on a tray. Eat at room temperature on the day they are made.
fr-moqueca-de-peixe: Cut the fish fillets into large portions (approximately 150 g each). In a bowl, combine with the lime juice, half the garlic, and salt. Toss gently to coat. Marinate for 20–30 minutes in the refrigerator. The lime juice will begin to denature the surface proteins, giving the fish a slightly opaque look and a more flavourful surface.

In a heavy clay pot (ideal) or wide, heavy-bottomed pan, pour the dendê oil. Layer the onion rounds across the base, then the tomato rounds, then the pepper strips, then the chilli. This layered approach is traditional — the vegetables cook in sequence from the heat of the oil below.

Lay the marinated fish pieces on top of the layered vegetables. Pour the coconut milk over everything — it should nearly submerge the fish. Cover tightly and cook over medium heat for 15–20 minutes, without stirring, until the fish is just cooked through and the coconut milk has combined with the vegetable juices and palm oil to create a brilliant orange-red broth. Add most of the coriander in the final 2 minutes. Taste and adjust salt.
fr-moroccan-chermoula-fish: Combine all chermoula ingredients in a food processor or pound in a large mortar. Process until a thick, bright-green paste forms — it should have body and cling to a spoon, not be a smooth liquid. Taste: it should be intensely herby, sour from the preserved lemon, and earthy-warm from the cumin. A traditional chermoula made in a mortar will have more texture; a processor gives a smoother result. Both are correct.

Score the fish deeply on both sides — 4–5 diagonal cuts per side, down to the bone. This is essential for two reasons: it allows the chermoula to penetrate deep into the flesh, and it prevents the skin from buckling in the oven. Rub two-thirds of the chermoula aggressively into every surface of the fish: inside the body cavity, into every score cut, and over the skin. Marinate for at least 30 minutes at room temperature, or up to 4 hours in the refrigerator.

Place the fish on a lightly oiled baking sheet or in a tagine. Spoon the reserved chermoula over the top. Bake at 200°C (400°F) for 20–25 minutes depending on thickness (10 minutes per 2.5cm of thickness at the widest point). The fish is done when the score cuts have opened and the flesh inside is white and opaque, and the skin is lightly blistered. Rest 5 minutes before serving. Garnish with lemon wedges and fresh cilantro.
fr-moroccan-lamb-tagine: In a large bowl, toss the lamb chunks with the grated onion, ras el hanout, ground ginger, and bloomed saffron water. Mix thoroughly to coat every surface. The onion will begin to break down from the salt in the spices and coat the lamb in a fragrant, slightly wet paste. Cover and marinate for at least 30 minutes at room temperature, or up to 24 hours refrigerated. The longer the marinate, the deeper the spice penetration into the meat.

Heat olive oil in a tagine base or heavy Dutch oven over medium-high heat until shimmering. Remove the marinated lamb from the bowl, scraping off excess onion paste (set it aside — it goes in next). Sear the lamb in batches, without crowding, for 3–4 minutes per side until deeply browned. The spice coating will caramelize and form an aromatic mahogany crust. Do not rush this step — proper browning provides the structural complexity the long braise builds upon.

Add the reserved onion paste to the pan and cook over medium heat for 5 minutes until softened. Return the seared lamb and any resting juices. Add the apricots, preserved lemon rind, and stock — the liquid should reach halfway up the lamb pieces, not submerge them. Bring to a simmer, then cover tightly (use foil under the lid for a better seal) and reduce heat to the lowest possible simmer. Cook for 1 hour 45 minutes to 2 hours, checking every 30 minutes and turning the meat once, until the lamb is falling off the bone and the sauce has reduced to a richly flavored, slightly syrupy consistency.

Taste the sauce and adjust — it should be complex, sweet-sour-savory, with the preserved lemon providing background brightness. If too sweet, add a squeeze of fresh lemon. If too thin, simmer uncovered on medium for 5–10 minutes with the lid off. Scatter fresh cilantro and toasted almond slivers over the surface just before serving. Serve in the tagine or Dutch oven directly at the table with rice, gluten-free flatbread, and harissa on the side.
fr-moroccan-lamb-tagine-nf: In a large bowl, toss the lamb chunks with the grated onion, ras el hanout, ground ginger, and bloomed saffron water. Mix thoroughly to coat every surface. The onion will begin to break down from the salt in the spices and coat the lamb in a fragrant, slightly wet paste. Cover and marinate for at least 30 minutes at room temperature, or up to 24 hours refrigerated. The longer the marinate, the deeper the spice penetration into the meat.

Bring to a simmer, then cover tightly (use foil under the lid for a better seal) and reduce heat to the lowest possible simmer. Taste the sauce and adjust — it should be complex, sweet-sour-savory, with the preserved lemon providing background brightness. If too sweet, add a squeeze of fresh lemon. If too thin, simmer uncovered on medium for 5–10 minutes with the lid off. Scatter fresh cilantro and toasted sunflower seeds slivers over the surface just before serving. Serve in the tagine or Dutch oven directly at the table with rice, gluten-free flatbread, and harissa on the side.
fr-moroccan-roasted-carrots: Preheat the oven to 200°C (400°F). In a large bowl, toss the halved carrots with olive oil, cumin, coriander, smoked paprika, cinnamon, salt, and pepper. Make sure every surface is coated in oil and spice. Arrange cut-side down on a large baking sheet in a single layer with space between each carrot — crowding causes steaming rather than roasting. Roast for 25–30 minutes until the cut sides are deeply caramelized and the edges show char spots.

Whisk together the harissa paste and honey into a smooth, rust-red glaze. Flip the partially roasted carrots cut-side up. Using a pastry brush or spoon, coat the cut side of each carrot generously with the harissa-honey glaze. Return to the oven for 8–10 more minutes until the glaze is bubbling, caramelized at the edges, and sticky. The sugar in the honey and the natural sugars in the carrots should reach deep caramelization — dark, almost jewel-like.

Transfer the glazed carrots to a serving plate, glaze-side up. Scatter the toasted pumpkin seeds over the carrots. Tear or roughly chop the fresh cilantro and scatter it over. A final drizzle of good olive oil finishes the dish. Serve warm or at room temperature — these are excellent both ways. At room temperature the glaze sets slightly and becomes almost candy-like in texture.
fr-moules-mariniere: Scrub each mussel under cold running water with a stiff brush to remove any barnacles and grit. Pull off the beard (the fibrous string protruding from the seam) by gripping it and pulling sharply toward the hinge end — pulling the other way tears the mussel. Tap any open mussel sharply on the counter: if it does not close within 10 seconds, discard it — it is dead. Discard any with cracked or broken shells. The mussels should smell purely of the ocean — clean, briny, and cool.

In a large, wide pot with a tight-fitting lid, melt half the butter over medium heat. Add the shallots, garlic, and bay leaf. Cook gently for 3–4 minutes, stirring, until the shallots are completely soft and translucent — they should not color at all. This short, gentle sweat is the flavor base and the moisture from the mussels will build on it. Season with pepper — no salt yet; the mussels will season the broth.

Raise the heat to high. Pour in the wine — it will spit and steam instantly. Let it boil hard for 1 minute to drive off the raw alcohol. Tip in all the cleaned mussels at once. Clamp the lid on tightly and cook on high heat for 3–4 minutes, shaking the pot vigorously once or twice by gripping the handles and swirling it in a circle. Open the lid after 3 minutes — nearly all mussels should be open. Cook another minute if needed. Discard any that remain closed after 5 minutes.

Remove the pot from heat. Add the remaining cold butter and swirl the pot to melt it into the broth — do not stir, just swirl, which emulsifies the butter into a slightly creamy, glossy broth. Add the parsley and give one final swirl. Taste the broth and adjust for pepper — the mussels will have seasoned it with salt. Divide into warmed deep bowls, making sure the broth is ladled over each portion generously. Serve immediately with gluten-free bread or frites.
fr-mujadara: Heat two-thirds of the olive oil in a wide, heavy skillet over medium heat. Add all sliced onions with a pinch of salt. Cook, stirring every 3–4 minutes, for 35–45 minutes total — patience here is not optional. The onions will reduce dramatically: first they release water and become translucent (15 min), then they will start to color (25 min), then darken and concentrate into a rich mahogany sweetness (35–45 min). Do not rush with high heat — the sugars must caramelize slowly.

In a separate small saucepan, heat remaining olive oil over medium-high. Add shallot rings — the oil should sizzle immediately. Fry, stirring often, for 8–10 minutes until rings are deeply golden and just beginning to darken. They will crisp as they cool, so remove them when still slightly flexible. Drain on paper towels. They turn crispy within 2 minutes of draining.

In the same caramelized-onion pot (with the onions still in it minus the reserved portion), add lentils and cover with water or stock. Add cumin and allspice. Bring to a boil, then simmer for 15 minutes until lentils are about two-thirds cooked — still with a slight firmness. Season with salt at this point.

Stir in the rinsed rice. Ensure there is enough liquid to cook the rice — about 1.5 cm above the surface of the lentil-rice mixture. Bring back to a boil, then cover tightly with a lid and cook over very low heat for 15 minutes. Remove from heat, keep covered, and steam for 5 more minutes. Fluff gently with a fork. The lentils and rice should be cohesive but not mushy.
fr-mushroom-barley-risotto: Heat 30 ml of the oil in a wide, heavy pot over medium-high heat. Add the mushrooms in a single layer (in two batches if crowded) and leave undisturbed 4 minutes. Stir, then cook 4–6 minutes more until the released water has evaporated and the mushrooms are deeply browned. Add the thyme, soy sauce, and a pinch of pepper, toss 30 seconds, then transfer to a bowl. Leave the pot unwashed.

Lower the heat to medium and add the remaining 15 ml oil to the same pot. Cook the shallots 3–4 minutes until soft, add the garlic for 30 seconds, then add the barley. Stir 2–3 minutes so the grains toast and pick up the mushroom fond.

Add the wine and stir until almost fully absorbed, about 2 minutes. Add the hot stock one ladle (about 180 ml) at a time, stirring often and adding more when the pot looks nearly dry. Keep at a lively simmer. Barley takes 35–40 minutes — longer than rice — and won't get quite as creamy, so stir well to release its starch. Season with salt halfway through.

Off the heat, add the cold butter and grated cheese and beat vigorously with a wooden spoon for 30 seconds until glossy. Fold in two-thirds of the mushrooms. Rest 1 minute, loosen with a little stock if needed, then serve topped with the remaining mushrooms, parsley, and black pepper.

fr-mushroom-bourguignon: Heat olive oil in a wide, heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven over high heat until shimmering. Add mushrooms in a single layer — work in batches if needed. Season with salt and do not stir for 2 minutes. Allow the mushrooms to release their moisture and then re-absorb it, developing a deep mahogany sear on each cut face.

In the same pot over medium heat, add shallots. Cook, stirring occasionally, for 6–8 minutes until softened and golden at the edges. The shallots should be translucent throughout but still hold their shape. Scrape up any remaining fond with a wooden spoon as the shallots release their liquid.

Pour the red wine into the pot with the shallots and add the thyme and bay leaves. Raise heat to medium-high and bring to a boil. Reduce the wine by half, about 8–10 minutes. This cooks off alcohol, concentrates fruit, and allows the tannins to mellow before the mushrooms rejoin.

Return the seared mushrooms to the pot, pour in the vegetable stock, and stir to combine. Bring to a gentle simmer, then reduce heat to low. Cover partially and cook for 40–45 minutes, stirring every 10 minutes. The liquid should maintain a slow, lazy bubble throughout — aggressive boiling will toughen the mushrooms.
fr-mushroom-risotto: Melt half the butter with the olive oil in a wide, heavy-bottomed pan over high heat. When foaming subsides, add the fresh mushrooms in a single layer — do not crowd them or they will steam and grey rather than roast. Cook without stirring for 2 to 3 minutes until deeply golden on the bottom, then toss and cook 2 more minutes. Add the garlic and thyme, toss 30 seconds, season with salt and pepper. Remove from the pan to a bowl and reserve. The mushrooms will go back in at the finish.

In the same pan, melt the remaining butter over medium heat. Add the shallots and sweat gently for 4 to 5 minutes until soft and translucent — no browning. Add the dry Carnaroli rice and stir continuously for 1 to 2 minutes until every grain turns translucent and picks up a faint nutty smell. This tostatura seals the outside of the grain, slowing starch release for a creamy-yet-al-dente finish. Add the white wine all at once and stir until completely absorbed.

Begin adding the warm mushroom stock — including the strained porcini soaking liquid — one ladle at a time. After each addition, stir constantly until the stock is almost fully absorbed before adding the next ladle. The starches released from the Carnaroli grains need this constant agitation to build the surrounding creamy matrix. This process takes 16 to 18 minutes over steady medium heat. Taste after 14 minutes — the rice should be just approaching al dente. Season with salt as you go. Keep the stock warm in a separate pan; cold stock shocks the rice and breaks the rhythm.

Pull the pan completely off the heat. Add the reserved sautéed mushrooms and fold them through. Then add the cold butter (cubed) and the Parmigiano all at once. Stir vigorously in a circular motion — this is the mantecatura, the moment where the fat from the cold butter emulsifies with the starchy cooking liquid to create the glossy, creamy sauce. Season to taste. The risotto should flow on the plate like a wave — not stand in a pile, not pour like soup. This is all'onda and it requires the risotto to be slightly looser than you think, because it sets on the plate.
fr-mushroom-stroganoff: This is the most important step and the most commonly botched. Heat a wide, heavy skillet — cast iron ideal — over high heat until it smokes. Add half the butter. When the foam subsides and the butter begins to brown, add the mushrooms in a single layer. Do NOT stir. Do not add all the mushrooms at once if they crowd the pan — do them in two or three batches. Let them sit and sear, undisturbed, for 2–3 minutes until a deep brown crust forms on the underside, then turn them. Initially the mushrooms release a large amount of liquid; this is normal. Stay on high heat and let that liquid evaporate completely. The sound in the pan changes from a steam-hiss to a sizzle when the moisture is gone — that is your cue. The mushrooms should be deeply browned, about 70% reduced in volume, their edges slightly crisped. Season with salt and pepper and transfer to a plate.

Reduce the heat to medium. Add the remaining butter to the same pan — the brown fond on the base will immediately begin to release into the butter, darkening it beautifully. Add the shallots and thyme and cook, stirring regularly, for 5–6 minutes until the shallots are soft and golden. Add the garlic and cook 1 minute more. Pour in the brandy — step back as it may flame briefly if the pan is hot enough. Scrape the base of the pan vigorously as the brandy reduces to almost nothing in about 1 minute. Pour in the stock and return the seared mushrooms to the pan. Simmer for 5 minutes until the stock has reduced by about half and the liquid is slightly thickened and glossy.

Reduce the heat to the absolute lowest setting — sour cream must never boil or it will split and curdle into grainy, broken lumps. Add the Dijon mustard to the pan and stir through. Spoon in the sour cream and fold it gently through the sauce in slow, wide strokes. Let it warm through for 1–2 minutes, barely simmering — the surface should shiver gently but never bubble actively. The sauce will turn from brown to a warm, pale buff colour as the cream is incorporated. Taste and adjust salt and pepper carefully — the reduction will have concentrated the saltiness already. The finished sauce should be creamy, tangy from the sour cream, warmly savory from the mushrooms, and bright from the mustard.

Add the cooked, drained egg noodles directly into the pan with the sauce and toss to coat every strand. If the sauce is too thick to coat the noodles freely, add a splash of gluten-free pasta cooking water to loosen — it emulsifies beautifully with the cream. Divide into warm bowls and shower generously with freshly chopped flat-leaf parsley. Serve with nothing more than a grinding of black pepper and a simple green salad. The noodles should be enrobed, not drowning; each strand should carry a visible, creamy coating.
fr-new-york-cheesecake: Combine the graham cracker crumbs and melted butter in a bowl and mix until the crumbs are evenly moistened — they should look like wet sand and hold together when squeezed. Press firmly into the bottom of a 23cm springform pan using the flat bottom of a measuring cup. Press firmly and evenly — including 2–3cm up the sides. Bake at 175°C for 8–10 minutes until just set. Cool completely before filling.

All ingredients must be at room temperature — cold cream cheese will not beat smooth and will leave lumps that never fully incorporate. Beat the cream cheese with a stand mixer paddle (not whisk) on medium speed until completely smooth and creamy, about 2 minutes. Scrape the bowl and beater thoroughly. Add the sugar and beat for 2 more minutes. Scrape again. Beat in the vanilla and salt. The goal is smooth — not airy. High-speed beating incorporates air that causes cracking.

With the mixer on low speed, add the eggs one at a time, beating only until each is just incorporated before adding the next — no more. Overmixing after adding eggs develops the batter and adds air. Finally, add the sour cream and mix on low just until combined. Scrape the bowl one final time and fold gently by hand with a spatula. The finished batter should be smooth, thick, and flow slowly.

Preheat oven to 160°C. Wrap the outside of the springform pan tightly in two layers of heavy foil (to prevent water ingress). Pour the batter into the cooled crust. Set the pan in a larger roasting pan and pour boiling water into the roasting pan to come halfway up the sides of the springform. Bake for 60–70 minutes until the edges are set and the center 10cm jiggles as a single mass. Turn off oven, crack door 5cm, and leave for 1 hour.

Remove from the water bath after the oven rest. Run a thin knife around the inside edge of the springform to release the cheesecake (this prevents cracking as it shrinks). Cool at room temperature for 2 hours. Refrigerate uncovered for at least 4 hours, ideally overnight. Remove the springform ring only when the cheesecake is fully cold. Slice with a hot, dry knife for clean cuts.

fr-nibitashi: Bring a large pot of unsalted water to a rolling boil. Submerge the spinach stems first for 15 seconds, then push the leaves under and blanch for 30–45 seconds total. The water must be at a full rolling boil throughout — a weak boil steams instead of blanches and the color suffers. Transfer immediately to a bowl of ice water and leave for 1 full minute.

Combine dashi, soy sauce, and mirin in a small saucepan. Bring to a gentle simmer over medium heat. Taste — the broth should taste pleasantly salty and lightly sweet, slightly more assertive than you want the finished dish to be, because the greens will dilute it. Simmer for 2 minutes to cook off the raw mirin alcohol.

Add the squeezed blanched greens to the simmering broth. Gently submerge them and simmer for just 60 seconds — this opens the cell walls slightly to allow the broth to enter. Remove from heat and let the greens steep in the broth, off the heat, for 15 minutes as the liquid cools. Lift the greens out, squeeze gently again to remove excess broth, and cut into 4 cm lengths. Arrange in small mounds in serving bowls. Spoon a small amount of the steeping liquid over each portion and top with bonito flakes.

fr-okra-stew: Heat the palm oil in a heavy pot or Dutch oven over medium heat until it liquefies and shimmers — palm oil is solid at room temperature and needs a moment. Add the diced onion and whole or roughly chopped scotch bonnet. Fry, stirring occasionally, until the onion is soft, translucent, and beginning to take on color at the edges, about 7–8 minutes. The palm oil and onion together form the aromatic foundation of the stew. The kitchen will fill with the unmistakable, earthy fragrance of red palm oil — this is correct.

Add the fresh tomatoes and tomato paste to the pot. Stir to combine and increase heat slightly. Cook uncovered, stirring frequently, until the tomatoes have completely broken down and the mixture has reduced substantially — about 12–15 minutes. The critical sign you are looking for is the oil rising to the surface and pooling at the edges of the pot. In Nigerian cooking this is called 'the oil floating' and signals that the water from the tomatoes has been driven off and the stew base is properly fried and concentrated.

Add the ground crayfish, pre-soaked shredded stockfish, and stock or water. Stir thoroughly and taste — the crayfish adds an intense, oceanic umami note and a faint sweetness that is the backbone of West African stews. If using stockfish, it should be pre-soaked for 24–48 hours and is already softened; dried fish (e.g. eja osan) goes in dry and rehydrates in the pot. Bring to a gentle simmer and cook for 5 minutes to marry the flavors. Taste and begin adjusting salt at this stage.

Prepare the okra according to preferred texture: for a very slimy (draw) stew — traditional and prized in many regions — shred the okra by grating on a box grater or pulsing briefly in a food processor. For a less mucilaginous version with discrete rounds, slice crosswise into 1 cm coins. Both methods release the mucilage that thickens the stew; shredding releases far more and produces a denser, more viscous result. Whichever method you use, the okra should be cut just before adding to the pot to prevent oxidation.

Add the okra to the simmering base. Stir once to incorporate, then resist the urge to stir vigorously or frequently — excessive stirring breaks down the okra and makes the stew overly slimy rather than silky. Cook on medium-low heat for 8–12 minutes, stirring gently only 2–3 times, until the okra is fully tender and the stew has thickened to a viscous, glossy consistency. Taste and adjust salt. The stew should be thick enough to mound slightly on a spoon and should coat the back of it. Serve over fufu, pounded yam, eba, or steamed rice.
fr-olive-oil-lemon-cake: Heat the oven to 350°F (175°C). Grease a 9-inch (23 cm) round cake pan with olive oil and line the bottom with parchment. Zest both lemons directly into the granulated sugar in a large bowl, then rub the zest into the sugar with your fingertips for 1–2 minutes. Juice the lemons and set the juice aside; you need 45 ml for the batter and about 20 ml for the glaze.

Add the eggs to the lemon sugar and whisk vigorously for about 1 minute until pale and slightly thickened. Whisk in the olive oil in a slow stream so it emulsifies, then the milk and 45 ml of lemon juice. In a separate bowl, whisk the flour, baking powder, and salt; add to the wet ingredients and whisk gently just until no dry flour remains. Scrape into the pan and sprinkle the turbinado sugar evenly over the top.

Bake on the middle rack for 40–45 minutes, until the top is golden, the edges pull away from the pan, and a toothpick inserted in the center comes out clean or with a few moist crumbs. Cool in the pan 15 minutes, then run a knife around the edge and turn out onto a rack, right-side up.

Whisk the powdered sugar with about 20 ml of the reserved lemon juice until smooth and thick but pourable, adding juice drop by drop. When the cake has cooled to just warm (about 30 minutes on the rack), spoon the glaze over the top and let it drip down the sides. Let it set 15 minutes before slicing.

fr-one-pot-cherry-tomato-spaghetti: Use a 12-inch (30 cm) straight-sided skillet or wide braiser the spaghetti can lie flat in. Lay the dry spaghetti in the pan, then scatter over the tomatoes, onion, garlic, red pepper flakes and half the basil (whole leaves). Add the olive oil, salt and the cold water — the pasta should be just submerged.

Bring to a rolling boil over high heat. As soon as the pasta softens (about 2 minutes), start turning it with tongs every 30–60 seconds so it doesn't clump. Keep at a vigorous boil, uncovered, for 9–11 minutes, until the pasta is al dente and the water has reduced to a few tablespoons of glossy, orange-red sauce. Press some of the tomatoes against the side of the pan as they soften.

Off the heat, add the Parmesan, a drizzle of olive oil and a few grinds of black pepper, and toss vigorously for 30 seconds so the cheese emulsifies into the sauce. Let stand 2 minutes. Fold in the remaining torn basil, taste for salt, and serve with extra cheese.
